body:
Verified this in online demo. The following code doesn't produce an error:

``` js
/* eslint "id-length": "error" */
const query = location.query.q ? location.query.q : ''
```

But this one does:

``` js
/* eslint "id-length": "error" */
const query = location.query.q || ''
```

Should this rule check properties every time, or only on assignment anyways?
@jrajav can you please provide the exact output from ESLint?

Seems to me like this should only check the left hand side of assignments. There's no guarantee you have any control over the right hand side (i.e. could be the results of an API call, 3rd party library, etc.). So in my opinion `const query = location.query.q || ''` shouldn't be flagged either, as `query` is potentially the only part you have control over naming.

@nzakas There is no output to provide. ESLint exits without an error.

@kaicataldo You are correct, but 3rd party libraries are outside of scope of this rule.

@ilyavolodin Oh yeah, that was just a (maybe poor) example. I was just trying to illustrate that it doesn't make sense to me to have the rule warn for `location.query.q`, since that property key name length might not be in the author's control at all.
@kaicataldo That rule has an option (which is on by default), to check properties of objects. If you are working with 3rd party libraries, you can just turn off that option.

Right, maybe I'm just not explaining myself well - I was trying to say I think this rule should only check the left hand side of assignments in response to:

> Should this rule check properties every time, or only on assignment anyways?
Ahh.. Ok, sorry, misunderstood what you were saying.

@ilyavolodin he mentioned if he changed the code, then he got a warning. That's the output I was looking for. 

Do we know what the next steps are here?

Seems like we should be consistent in our treatment of

``` js
const query = location.query.q ? location.query.q : ''
```

and 

``` js
const query = location.query.q || ''
```

It makes sense to me to not warn at all for the right hand side, for the reasons mentioned above, so my vote is to not warn on either of the above. Maybe I'm missing something, though?
